title: What State Am I In? Census State Lookup
description: Answer 'What State Am I In?' against the Census state polygon — state FIPS, highlighted boundary and ACS population and income context. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a point in Kansas City is a coin flip between Kansas and Missouri until the Census polygon settles it — the river city straddles the line its name hides.
quick_answer: What State Am I In? checks a point against the U.S. Census Bureau state polygon and returns the state name, its FIPS code and a highlighted boundary, joined with recent ACS population, income, housing, age, education and poverty estimates. Search, GPS, coordinates or click — verified, not guessed.

faq: How does MapBench identify the state?
By testing the point against the U.S. Census Bureau's state polygon — official geometry, point-in-polygon. Search, GPS, coordinates and clicks all resolve to that one check.
What is a state FIPS code?
The two-digit Census code for the state (California 06, Texas 48, New York 36) — the prefix of every county FIPS in the state and a standard join key.
Where do the population and income figures come from?
The Census Bureau's American Community Survey — recent estimates for population, income, housing, age, education and poverty, shown with their survey nature intact.
Can I use GPS or coordinates?
Yes — GPS, address search, pasted coordinates or a map click all work; the verification is identical once the point is set.
Is this a legal boundary tool?
It applies the official public geometry and is a strong reference. Legal determinations rest with authorities and licensed surveys.
District of Columbia and territories?
DC resolves as the district it is (FIPS 11). Territories follow their own geographies beyond the state framework.
A point on a state-line river?
Polygons follow the legal line (often mid-channel or a bank, per the states' compacts) — the Census geometry decides, and split cases are exactly its job.
Why show estimates rather than the census count?
Because between censuses the ACS is the current official picture. Counts age; estimates update — labelled as estimates.
State historical boundaries?
States have moved rarely but really (West Virginia's birth the famous case). Current geometry is this page's scope.
Puerto Rico and territories?
They resolve through their own Census geographies where covered — the state framework's edges are handled as the data holds them, labelled plainly.
My GPS drift says the next state.
Consumer GPS near a border can straddle it. Average your position outdoors for a few seconds; the polygon verdict follows the settled point.
